title: Nico, Ada, and the Missing Piece
markdown:
The Campus Chronicle office buzzed on deadline nights. Stale coffee thickened the air. Keyboards kept a frantic rhythm. Dawn was a rival they meant to beat, and usually the race had a shine. Tonight Nico the jackdaw meant to make that shine intentional.

Nico was a language student who used three adjectives when one would do, and used them well. He fluttered in, iridescent feathers catching the harsh overheads like small rainbows, and began rearranging stacks with a decisive flick of beak, as if conducting a feathered orchestra. He wanted polish and intelligence: ideas like cut gems, sentences with elegant precision. He had brought a small ornate inkwell, the sort one expected in a philosopher’s study, as if it might preside over the night like a scholarly maestro.

“Right,” he announced, voice crisp through the murmur. “An atmosphere of dignified productivity. A gentle cadence, if you will, not a frantic scrabble.” He adjusted rejected articles and sighed as if disarray were a personal insult. “The objective is something significant. Something that resonates with intellectual depth.”

The door creaked and admitted a different weather. Ada the cat busker moved with a fluid grace that ignored the office chaos, fur the colour of twilight after a summer storm, eyes like twin emeralds. She carried a battered, well-loved ukulele case that had seen more miles than a seasoned explorer. Ada did not deal in polished prose. She dealt in rhythm, in the raw honest sound of a story being told, the pulse of a city corner and a crowd’s heartbeat.

She surveyed Nico’s carefully proofread stack, the other students hunched over glowing screens, the mild panic hovering like a misplaced punctuation mark, and a slow knowing smile found her whiskers. She claimed a quiet corner, unpacked, and began to strum a soft melancholic melody. It cut the tension like a warm breeze on a chilly evening. Not loud. Not showy. It had the depth of late nights on street corners, stories whispered to indifferent stars.

Nico, naturally, found this distracting. A pointed glance, a subtle frown, a ripple in his composure. “A rather vocal interpretation of dignified productivity, wouldn’t you say?”

Ada winked. The low steady rhythm continued. “My production, darling. Keeps the jitters from turning into full-blown panic. Plus, someone needs to remind us there is more to life than apostrophes and immaculate footnotes.” She gave a little flourish; a nearby potted plant trembled.

Nico shuffled papers, adjusted imaginary spectacles, and reviewed the whole layout in his mind. He envisioned sleek intelligence, journalistic rigor, a beacon of academic excellence in the messy world of student publications. He was practically shining with imagined prestige.

Then Percy shrieked. A sound like a paper cut to the soul. Wings flapped. Feathers flew. “No. No, no.” Percy wailed and scattered a few stray feathers that looked, for a moment, like misplaced commas.

Nico glided over, beak parting, carefully constructed composure shattering like cheap glass. Ada’s strumming faltered for a single beat, then continued a little more somber, concern woven through the line. There it was. Not a typo, not a grammatical slip, not a comma on holiday. Worse. The lead article, the one Nico had championed for intellectual weight, had gone to print without its concluding paragraph. It simply stopped. Mid-sentence. A story ripped from its last page, the reader left hanging in the void.

The room fell quiet except for Ada’s lament and the frantic beating of Percy’s wings. A chill crept up Nico’s iridescent feathers, nothing to do with the drafty office. All the careful planning, the atmosphere of superiority, had culminated in this chasm in their most important piece. The journalistic equivalent of tripping on stage during an acceptance speech.

He looked at the stark white space where words should have been, then at Ada’s steely, kind gaze. Steam rose around serious faces and discarded paper cups. Despair, cold and metallic, washed him to the quills. He had aimed for a symphony and got a broken note.

“I asked for subtlety and received a banner,” he whispered, bitter. The banner was the error: colossal, unmissable. He imagined headlines, whispers, the Chronicle’s ruined name and, by extension, his own.

Ada stopped strumming. She walked over, tail a gentle swish, and placed a paw on his wing, feather-light and grounding. “It happens, birdy. The world is not always perfectly edited. Sometimes the best stories are the ones you patch up as you go. Think of it as a really challenging crossword, only with more people reading your answers.”

Nico looked at her, really looked, for the first time that evening. Not the chaotic busker who had disrupted his orchestration, but someone who understood the messiness of making, the inevitable imperfections of bringing something new into the world. Someone who did not pretend everything was always perfect. Someone real.

“The reputation,” he stammered. “The credibility of the paper. Mine.”

Ada nudged his wing. “Reputations are built on more than avoiding mistakes. They are built on how you fix them. And sometimes a little honesty goes a lot further than a lot of gloss. People respect a straight answer, even a slightly wobbly one.”

Gadzooks, that was the turn. Nico, who had craved polish and the illusion of effortless brilliance, saw the grit in knowing what to do when the illusion shattered. Face the mess. Make it better. Do not pretend the mess never happened.

They spent the next hour without miracles or a theatrical save. They worked. Ada, with her knack for the heart of a thing, helped him rephrase the missing conclusion. They did not try to make it groundbreaking or particularly witty. They made it clear and honest. Percy, surprisingly, found a forgotten interview snippet in his notes that added a crucial piece of context, a footnote that clarified the whole. They worked with a shared purpose that outlasted their first impressions. The frantic scrabble became a steady determined rhythm, a band playing something heartfelt after all.

Morning striped the worn linoleum. The Chronicle lay on the newsstands, complete. The leading article ended differently than planned, with a brief humble note that admitted the oversight and, paradoxically, made the piece feel more trustworthy. It was not the flawless masterpiece Nico had envisioned. It was something better. Honest. Fixed.

He perched on the windowsill and watched students pick up the paper, faces unbothered by the subtle amendment, engrossed in the news itself. Peace settled deep. He had learned, not in a lecture hall but in the messy heart of a deadline, that polish without substance is a beautiful feather with no bird attached—and that the impressive move is to admit the miss and mend it with taste, honesty, and proportion, while a street-smart cat provides the soundtrack. The ornate inkwell, unused as a maestro’s prop, still sat on the desk, ordinary and sufficient, a little dark mouth that no longer needed to preside.
audience: young adults aged 16-18, teen anthology entry
